source_refs.note: Exercise 10.1, Question 8: book page 278 (Q1-Q24). The book prints no answers for Exercise 10.1.

blocks.explanation:
Two different ratios appear; the identity \(\csc^{2}x = 1 + \cot^{2}x\) leaves only \(\cot x\).
Then \(\cot^{2}x = \frac{1}{3}\), i.e. \(\tan x = \pm\sqrt{3}\).
Plan: solve with period \(\pi\); check that \(\cot x\), \(\csc x\) are defined.
steps:
Given: \(3\cot^{2}x + 3\csc^{2}x = 5\).
To find: principal solutions and general solution.
Method: use \(\csc^{2}x = 1 + \cot^{2}x\) to get one ratio, then solve for \(\tan x\).

Change to tangent
\[\tan^{2}x = 3\]
\[\tan x = \pm\sqrt{3}\]
Why: \(\tan x = \frac{1}{\cot x}\); square root with two signs.

Solve (reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\))
\[\tan x = \sqrt{3}:\ x = \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\]
\[\tan x = -\sqrt{3}:\ x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\]
Why: positive tangent in quadrants I, III; negative in II, IV (as in Question 6).

Are \(\cot x\) and \(\csc x\) defined?
At none of these angles is \(\sin x = 0\), so all four are valid.
Why: \(\cot x = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\) and \(\csc x = \frac{1}{\sin x}\) need \(\sin x \ne 0\).

General solution
The period of \(\tan x\) is \(\pi\):
\[\left\{\dfrac{\pi}{3} + n\pi\right\}\]
\[\cup \left\{\dfrac{2\pi}{3} + n\pi\right\},\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\]
Why: \(\frac{4\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{3} + \pi\) and \(\frac{5\pi}{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3} + \pi\).

Check
\[x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}:\ 3\cdot\dfrac{1}{3} + 3\cdot\dfrac{4}{3} = 1 + 4 = 5\]
Why: \(\cot\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), \(\csc\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\); the squares are the same at the other three angles.
blocks.final_answer: Principal solutions in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(x = \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{2\pi}{3}, \frac{4\pi}{3}, \frac{5\pi}{3}\). General solution: \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{3} + n\pi\right\}\) \(\cup\) \(\left\{\frac{2\pi}{3} + n\pi\right\}\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The textbook prints no answers for Exercise 10.1. Every answer on this page is ours: worked out step by step, checked independently with a computer algebra system (sympy) and compared with a solution book. As in the book's examples, we give the principal solutions in \([0, 2\pi]\) and the general solution as a union of sets.
